name: Lena Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the egg side at Brookend, which is sixteen thousand free-range hens in four sheds, plus a bit of wheat and some beef cattle the owners keep out of habit. My day starts at half five with a walk through every shed before the pop-holes open, the little doors that let the hens out to range. I'm listening more than looking. A happy shed has a sort of low chatter, and an unhappy one goes quiet or shrieky, and you learn the difference over twenty years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Then it's the packing room. The eggs come in on belts and two of my team, Grace and Mehmet, grade them and stack the trays for the lorry from the packer, which comes at eleven. After that it's floor eggs, fencing, the fox, the paperwork for the inspector. I have three people under me and I'm paid about what a supermarket shift manager gets, which my sister reminds me of every Christmas.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology in all this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Some. The sheds have sensors for temperature and ammonia, and I check them on my phone. I use one of the AI chat things now and then, mostly to tidy up a stiff letter to the packer when they've docked our price again. I don't trust it with anything about the birds. It doesn't know a hen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful little tool and leave it there. In the packing room Grace would say her son uses it for everything and I'd say good for him. Nobody would get worked up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it changes almost nothing. The thing that decides my year is the egg price the packer sets, and the feed price, and bird flu. AI as a better search engine doesn't touch any of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it a bit more for the letters and the forms, maybe the grant applications, which take me whole evenings. That might give me back two evenings a month with Sami and the kids. Apart from that, carry on, keep the hens alive, keep asking for a pay review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly relieved, if anything, that the paperwork might get a bit lighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned bird flu. What happens to you if it hits Brookend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then all sixteen thousand birds are killed on the spot and the sheds sit empty for months. The owners get compensation for the birds, but my bonus is gone and two of my team go on short hours. It happened to a farm twelve miles away last year and I drove past their empty sheds every day for weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those two evenings back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Sit down. Noor's fourteen and she's started talking to me properly again in the car, so maybe I'd do the driving to her netball instead of Sami. Small things.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful little tool and leave it there. Grace would say her son uses it for everything, and nobody in the packing room would get worked up.
S0.think: I think it changes almost nothing for me. My year is decided by the egg price from the packer, the feed price and bird flu, and AI doesn't touch any of those.
S0.do: Uses AI a bit more for letters, forms and grant applications, hoping to win back two evenings a month for her family. Otherwise keeps the hens well and keeps asking for a pay review.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little relieved that the paperwork might lighten.
S0.quote: It happened to a farm twelve miles away last year and I drove past their empty sheds every day for weeks.
S0.fieldNote: She's measured and practical, and she measures risk in hens, not in jobs. Bird flu is the real fear in her life, far bigger than AI here. The detail about Noor talking to her in the car showed what she'd spend saved time on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've seen this before with machines, the work changes slowly and the bosses use it as an excuse to hire fewer young people. I'd say we need apprenticeships that are paid properly, not cheap labour dressed up as training. I'd post that on the regional farmers' group, and get the usual three angry replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the packer would use it first, to set prices tighter and check our records faster, and that hurts me more than any robot. They already squeeze us. A clever system on their side and a tired woman with a laptop on mine is not a fair fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the course the farming college runs on farm software, once a few people I know had done it and said it was worth it. It's three evenings, and the fee's about a hundred and fifty, which I'd ask the owners to pay. And I'd talk to the other egg producers about selling together, so we're not each facing the packer alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit tired of always being the smaller side of every deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling together with other producers, is that something you've tried before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We tried in 2019, five farms. It fell apart in a year because two of them couldn't agree on who'd do the books. This time, maybe the books are the part a machine could do, and then there's less to argue about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the hiring fewer beginners part, does that touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mehmet's my youngest at twenty-two, and he'd never have got in if I hadn't pushed for him. If the owners think a system can cover some of his work, they'll say no next time. I'd fight it, but I'd lose.

S1.say: I'd say we've seen this before: work changes slowly and bosses use it as an excuse to hire fewer young people. We need properly paid apprenticeships, and I'd post that on the regional farmers' group.
S1.think: I think the packer would use it first to set prices tighter and check our records faster. A clever system on their side against a tired woman with a laptop on mine isn't a fair fight.
S1.do: Signs up for the college's three-evening farm software course once friends say it's worth it, asking the owners to cover the fee of about a hundred and fifty. Talks to other egg producers about selling together again.
S1.feel: Uneasy, and tired of always being the smaller side of the deal.
S1.quote: A clever system on their side and a tired woman with a laptop on mine is not a fair fight.
S1.fieldNote: Her steadiness shows clearly: she'd take the course, but only after others have tried it. She sees the threat as power shifting to the packer, not robots in her sheds. Her idea that a machine could do the books that broke up the old group was a nice turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in now, with retraining and support, not after a million people are out of work. I'd say the AI firms should pay into it. I'd probably write to our local representative, which I've done twice before about bird flu compensation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly other people's trouble, but it lands on me sideways. Sami drives the town bus, and if the offices thin out, there are fewer people on his route. And the packer's office staff go, which means my calls go to a machine, and I hate that already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Sami to look at the bus company's plans and whether his union's saying anything. I'd cut the second car, which would save us maybe two hundred a month, and share with my neighbour Ruth on school runs. And I'd keep a printed copy of every contract with the packer, because I'd want proof if a machine changes the terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, edging toward worried. It's like hearing that the flu is three farms away instead of thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cutting the second car is a big step. Why that first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the only big thing we can cut that doesn't touch the kids. The mortgage is fixed, the food is the food. Idris would complain about the walk to the bus stop, but he's ten, he'll survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep printed contracts. Has the packer changed terms on you before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice. Once they changed the size grades by two grams and it cost us about four percent overnight, and it was in an email I'd skimmed. Now I print everything and read it with a pen, like my mother did with the electricity bill.

S2.say: I'd say the government must step in now with retraining and support, before a million people are out of work, and the AI firms should pay into it. I'd write to our local representative again.
S2.think: I think it's mostly other people's trouble, but it lands on me sideways. My partner's bus route would empty as offices thin out, and my calls to the packer would go to a machine.
S2.do: Gets her partner to check his bus company's plans and union, cuts the second car to save about two hundred a month, and shares school runs with her neighbour Ruth. Prints and reads every packer contract with a pen.
S2.feel: Uneasy edging toward worried, like hearing the flu is three farms away instead of thirty.
S2.quote: It's like hearing that the flu is three farms away instead of thirty.
S2.fieldNote: She plans in a calm, orderly way and cuts the one big cost that doesn't touch the kids. The printed contracts come from a real sting, the two-gram grade change. Her worry here is mostly about her partner's job and her family's margins, not her own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to decide who this country is for. If shares and houses boom while people lose their jobs, the gains have to be shared, through tax, through a proper safety net. I'd go to the rally in town, and I'd bring Noor, because she should see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm all right in the short run, the hens don't care about any of it. But we have a mortgage and no savings, so a house boom only helps people who already own lots. And when lots of professionals lose their jobs, they stop paying extra for free-range eggs and buy the cheap ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with the owners in the first month and look at what happens if free-range demand drops by a fifth, because I think it would. I'd suggest we turn one shed to barn eggs, which are cheaper to produce, before we're forced to. And I'd start using the AI tool properly for the numbers, because by then everyone sensible would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. I'm better when there's a plan on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bring Noor to the rally. What would you want her to take from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That things don't just happen to you, people decide them. My grandmother marched for the hospital in our town and it's still open. I want Noor to know that's a thing you can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd switch a shed to barn eggs. How do you feel about that, as someone who cares about the birds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hate it, honestly. Barn hens never see the sky. But a farm that goes bust looks after no hens at all, and I'd rather keep three sheds outdoors than lose all four.

S3.say: I'd say this is the moment to decide who the country is for, and booming gains must be shared through tax and a proper safety net. I'd go to the town rally and bring my daughter.
S3.think: I think I'm all right short term because hens don't care. But with a mortgage and no savings the house boom does nothing for me, and laid-off professionals would stop buying free-range eggs.
S3.do: Meets the owners in the first month to plan for free-range demand falling by a fifth and proposes turning one shed to barn eggs early. Starts using AI properly for the farm's numbers.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, steadier once there's a plan on the kitchen table.
S3.quote: But a farm that goes bust looks after no hens at all, and I'd rather keep three sheds outdoors than lose all four.
S3.fieldNote: She spotted a second-order effect most farmers wouldn't: laid-off professionals buy cheaper eggs. Her values and her business sense pulled against each other over the barn shed, and she admitted it openly. Bringing her daughter to the rally ties her politics to family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms have to come with rules: who owns them, who's responsible when they hurt an animal, and what happens to the people they replace. I'd say it at every meeting going. I'd sign up to the union campaign, even though I've never been very active.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think egg farms go first. The collection's already on belts, and a robot that picks floor eggs and walks the sheds at night is exactly what the owners would buy. Grace, Mehmet and Tom would be gone within two years, and I'd be the one telling them. Then I'd be next, or I'd be managing machines for less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owners straight out what their plan is, and get it on paper. I'd learn the robots once the first farms had them running, because I'd rather be the person who manages them than the person who's replaced. I'd go to Sami's union meeting with him, and I'd stop the kids' extra swimming lessons to get something saved, even a few hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I keep thinking of that empty shed twelve miles away, but with all the hens still inside and nobody I know in there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one telling Grace and Mehmet. Can you picture that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can. Grace has been with me eleven years, and she'd say, Lena, you promised. Because I did, after the flu scare, I said we'd always need people. I'd have to stand in the packing room and say I was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the robots, but you're also scared. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, every day. I'd learn them because the mortgage doesn't care how I feel. But I'd go home and cry in the car some nights, before I went in to the kids.

S4.say: I'd say farm robots need rules on ownership, on responsibility when they hurt an animal, and on support for replaced workers. I'd say it at every meeting and join the union campaign.
S4.think: I think egg farms go first, since collection is on belts and a shed-walking robot is exactly what the owners would buy. My team would go within two years, and I'd be next or managing machines for less.
S4.do: Asks the owners for their plan in writing and learns to run the robots once other farms have them working. Goes to her partner's union meeting and stops the kids' extra swimming to save a few hundred.
S4.feel: Scared, picturing full sheds with nobody she knows inside, and torn between coping and grief.
S4.quote: Grace has been with me eleven years, and she'd say, Lena, you promised.
S4.fieldNote: This is where her steadiness gets tested. She'd still adapt, because the mortgage leaves no choice, but she carries real guilt about a promise to her team. The image of crying in the car before facing the kids was the most honest moment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, the last one, without a doubt. The others hurt people I love, but that one empties my sheds of people. What would help is a rule that farms using robots keep some staff and retrain them, paid, and help for families like ours with no savings, a bridge for a year so we're not making every choice in a panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the hens would make of it. That sounds silly. But they notice a stranger in the shed, they bunch up and go quiet, and I wonder how they'd take a machine walking through every night. Somebody should ask the people who know the animals before they decide.

headlineQuote: I'd learn them because the mortgage doesn't care how I feel. But I'd go home and cry in the car some nights, before I went in to the kids.
portrait: Lena Farah, 43, runs a sixteen-thousand-hen free-range egg unit with a team of three, on modest pay and with less than a month saved. She's careful and practical, using AI now and then for letters but never trusting it with the birds, and she adapts only once others have proven a thing works. Through the early scenarios she worries less about her own job than about the packer's power, her partner's bus route and falling demand for free-range eggs. In the robot scenario she expects egg farms to be first, would still learn the machines for the mortgage's sake, and feels deep guilt about having to let her team go.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and fast robots picture, because it would empty her sheds of people and she'd have to let her own team go.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that farms using robots keep and retrain some staff on pay, and a year-long bridge of support for families with no savings.
